newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Pound wipes out Glaxo sales gains.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pound wipes out Glaxo sales gains.

text.p: Britain's Glaxo Wellcome Plc (GW) said on Monday that the strong pound had wiped out a 10 percent rise in sales in the first four months of the year.

In his last speech as chairman, Sir Colin Corness told shareholders at the group's annual meeting that sales between January and April totalled 2.75 billion pounds, a gain of 10 percent at constant exchange rates but effectively flat because of sterling's advance.
And he added that if exchange rates remained at their present level for the rest of 1997 "the adverse impact on earnings for the whole year would be around five percent."
Glaxo Wellcome shares ended the session down 2.6 percent, or 31 1/2 pence, at 1251 1/2 pence.

However analysts noted that the decline followed a strong run in recent weeks, with Glaxo Wellcome touching an all-time high of 1299 pence last week as Britain's biggest drug groups benefited from increasing U.S. interest.

The stock was already down more than 20 pence ahead of the shareholder meeting, in line with Britain's other drug majors, Zeneca Group Plc and SmithKline Beecham Plc, reflecting nervousness about Wall Street's opening.
"All in all these (results) were good and nothing to get excited about," said an analyst at a U.S. bank in London.

GW, which faces the loss of the important U.S. patent on its one-time blockbuster ulcer drug Zantac this summer, repeated its bullish view that it will achieve single-digit sales growth in 1997 and 1998 and return to double-digit growth in 1999 as newer drugs fill the gap.
Respiratory drugs have now become the group's biggest-selling category, with Zantac sales dropping to 20 percent of group sales by the end of April compared with 43 percent in 1994.

"I don't think there is any great surprise in this statement," Panmure Gordon analyst Robin Gilbert said. "It is fairly encouraging - the company is saying (it) will overcome these problems of patent expires and there is optimism that they will do so."

Another analyst said he was pleasantly surprised by the rate of decline in Zantac sales, which the company has repeatedly warned could plunge by up to 90 percent when the drug is exposed to full competition.

He noted that overall Zantac sales were down only seven percent, despite a decline of more than 20 percent in U.S. prescriptions. "That would indicate the rest of the world is doing rather well," he said.
GW said sales of other products rose by 15 percent in the four-month period at constant exchange rates, with anti-viral and central nervous system products seeing strong growth.
Corness retired as chairman following Monday's meeting, with deputy chairman and chief executive Sir Richard Sykes succeeding him as executive chairman.
Sykes will hand over the chief executive post to the group's chief operating officer Sean Lance in May 1998.
